title: fMRI-Guided rTMS Doesn't Work For Everything
subtitle: A new randomized controlled trial for osteoarthritis knee pain shows no difference from sham treatment.
body_html:
The difference between science and non-science is that science is falsifiable. I love falsifiable hypotheses. Treatments that always work aren't real treatments. In today's quick dispatch, in keeping with my prior articles about how to read articles, we will review a negative trial.1

Accelerated intermittent theta burst transcranial magnetic stimulation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex for chronic knee osteoarthritis pain

What's a negative trial? It's a study in which the hypothesized intervention didn't do any better than the “placebo” (in the case of device or instrumentation trials, we are for that as a sham, not a placebo).

This newsletter covers neuromodulation because it's a personal area of enthusiasm. But it doesn't work all the time, and it doesn't work for everything. Today, additional data demonstrates that doing an extremely fancy fMRI-guided brain stimulation is not the right approach for knee pain. For those inclined to yell, “I could've told you that,” well, sure, but it's not science until you prove it.

We already know that aiTBS—a pattern of multiple “theta-burst” treatments with transcranial magnetic stimulation is effective in depression. It's the basis of SAINT neuromodulation, for example. We even have one FDA-cleared approach for peripheral pain management with neuromodulation, a protocol developed by colleagues at MagVenture. So this isn't totally crazy. We also know that osteoarthritis, as a source of pain, is a real problem. Most people who have osteoarthritis pain don't get a joint replacement, which is the definitive treatment for that sort of pain.

Only 18%–30% with OA undergo total knee replacement in their lifetime2

Direct high-frequency motor cortex stimulation has also been recommended, with level A evidence3, which is substantial. Keep in mind that the oral medication we have for pain either causes serious side effects or can cause life-ending dependence.

Given SAINT's success in depression, the authors took a similar approach to functional connectivity: guided accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation using the same intermittent and iTBS pattern.

The dosing was lower than used in depression, which is worth recalling because it's possible that they just underdosed the treatment:

Accelerated iTBS intervention was delivered over 4 days (V2-V5) each day consisting of 5 blocks (B1-B5) of stimulation (1800 pulses per block, 9000 pulses per visit/day, 36000 pulses in total/treatment week).

They also used a different functional connectivity target from that used in prior depression trials, in this case:

The optimal site was defined as the peak voxel within the lDLPFC receiving maximal effective connectivity from the right anterior insula (rAI; 6mm sphere centred on MNI voxel coordinates [x=30, y=24, z=-14]), abbreviated as rAI-connected lDLPFC (or rAIc-lDLPFC).

I can't tell you if this is the best site to use. I'm not an expert. One of the problems with reading this kind of paper is that you do benefit from being an expert in everything they're going to talk about to evaluate whether what they're doing makes any sense. And unfortunately, no one can be an expert in everything. I lack the expertise to answer, “Is the optimal connectivity site targeted reasonable for the outcome they sought?”

However, I got off the hook in this case because they found that it didn't work. So, whether it was a reasonable or unreasonable target matters a lot less because the answer was that it didn't work.

Or rather, it did work, but it worked whether they got sham or active treatment. Pain scores went down pretty dramatically in the active group, comparing pre-treatment and post-treatment assessments.

In the active group, significant mean changes from baseline were observed in NRS current pain (mean change difference -1.38 [95% CI 0.81], p=0.0016), NRS worst pain (-1.55 [1.00], p=0.0033), NRS average pain (-1.45 [0.78], p=0.0008),

And there were similar improvements across the number of endpoints in the sham group:

In the sham group, significant mean changes from baseline were observed in ICOAP constant pain (-17.50 [9.38], p=0.0177), ICOAP intermittent pain (-15.97 [9.29], p=0.0100),

However, looking at the primary point, the patient-reported outcome measures, there was no difference between groups:

However, there was no statistically significant between-group differences (active vs sham) in PROMS scores

Now, there is one quirk here. The sham they chose wasn't completely inactive. This is an error in the study design, in my opinion, and I only know that because I've read a lot of TMS studies. What they used for ham was a 30% power on the stimulator:

As no dedicated sham coil was available, sham intervention was given through the same coil. All pulses were delivered at 30% stimulator output and orienting the coil perpendicular to the scalp surface with direct contact.

There's a better sham that can be used! Drs. Cole and Williams used this alternate sham in the SAINT trial, and Dr. Mark George uses it routinely. Electrical zappers can be placed on your TMS coil so that it feels identically zappy to the participants but doesn't stimulate the brain because the magnetic surface of the coil is placed so far away from the patient's brain that It can't do anything. My free advice to subsequent investigators: if you're going through all the trouble of doing fMRI guidance in a TMS trial, write to the manufacturer and request a sham coil. They'll probably hook you up. Why is this a problem?

It may be that 30% powered iTBS is enough to have a treatment effect! That could be why there is no separation between these two groups, as both were effectively active. I have reasons to doubt this is the case. Still, it's not impossible, and I won't jump to replicate this negative study with a better sham control. Do you worry that the question is not as definitively answered as it could've been?

There we have it! Either elaborately fMRI-guided iTBS isn't different from sham in the treatment of osteoarthritis pain, or even low-power iTBS is effective.

One thing we can say is that placebo is fantastic. I'm happy it's around; it relieves more suffering than most treatments. Placebo, the power of feeling cared for, continues to be a remarkable treatment for alleviating human suffering.

We have to stay on guard because a placebo or sham is tremendously powerful, which is why we routinely compare it to it. But it's not an effect or treatment; it's a potent treatment, and that's why it keeps its role as the standard against which we measure in science.

2

Osteoarthritis Cartilage, 25 (4) (2017), pp. 455-461

3
